extracted.intended_audience: experimental biologists, physicians, and scientifically literate readers interested in microbiology and the historical/ methodological standards for testing spontaneous generation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and methodological criteria for designing, conducting, and interpreting experiments that test spontaneous generation (i.e., whether life arises without antecedent life). Emphasizes sterilization, air sampling/filtration, controls, aseptic technique, detection sensitivity, and the need to test alternative hypotheses and repeat under varied conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sterilization and hermetic sealing of samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Infusions boiled and flask necks sealed (Spallanzani; described method of filling, boiling, and sealing flasks so they remain hermetically closed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boil infusions to destroy existing life, then seal the neck (heat and close glass) so the flask is hermetically closed. Sealed flasks that remain clear on later inspection support absence of spontaneous generation; any breakage/opening that admits air must be accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air filtration and purity of supplied air
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing air through bulbs containing concentrated sulphuric acid or through water to remove/kill airborne germs (Schulze), and recognizing locality of the air matters for results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure filtration actually detains or destroys germs — passage must be slow enough to wet and contact floating matter. Water can be as effectual as sulphuric acid if contact is ensured. Consider ambient air purity (altitude, caves, plains) when interpreting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of porous plugs (cotton-wool) to filter incoming air
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing cotton-wool plugs to filter air supplied to infusions (Schroeder and Von Dusch) which in most cases prevented putrefaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cotton-wool filtering is effective in preventing airborne organisms from entering infusions, though exceptions may occur (e.g., milk). Report substrate-specific exceptions and test reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of airborne particulate/germinal matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Collecting floating particles of air, examining them microscopically, and showing air is not uniformly charged with organisms (Pasteur's collection and locality comparisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use active collection and microscopic sowing to detect organized particles. Compare air from different locations (glacier, caves, plains) to demonstrate non-uniform distribution of germinal matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of membranes to distinguish particulate from dissolved agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Separating sterilized infusion from putrefying one by a membrane that allows diffusion of liquid but prevents organisms (Helmholtz) to show putrefaction agent is particulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sterilized liquid remains unchanged while a putrefying liquid separated by a membrane causes no effect, infer the active agent is particulate and cannot pass the membrane — use membranes to test whether cause is dissolved vs particulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aseptic technique when opening/manipulating samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Sterilizing instruments (e.g., heating pliers in flame) before snipping flask necks; taking precautions to prevent contamination from operator or clothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before any opening/manipulation, sterilize tools in flame; stand leeward of flasks to avoid shedding dust; avoid directing particles from operator toward samples. Treat every opening as a potential contamination event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls, comparative and duplicate experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Running multiple flasks of the same infusion, exposing groups to different conditions (sealed vs opened; opened in hay-loft vs opened in mountain air), and comparing outcomes to identify contamination sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include parallel groups and replicate samples; differences between identical procedures in different locations or between sealed vs opened flasks indicate external germ sources. Use broken or intentionally opened flasks as positive contamination indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition, disciplined variation, and avoidance of theoretical bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Need for careful repetition, skillful variation of conditions, incessant questioning of results, and resistance to prepossession or advocacy (critique of Pouchet and praise for disciplined methods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to be repeatable and to explore variable space; avoid letting theoretical commitments drive sloppy experimental practice. Treat unexpected results with skepticism and attempt independent repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensitive detection methods (light beam and high-magnification microscopy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a concentrated beam of light as a searching test for suspended matter and microscopes of sufficient power (e.g., ~1000x) to reveal microorganisms that weaker optics miss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ optical tests more sensitive than unaided vision; inspect samples under high magnification and with light-scattering methods to confirm germlessness; recognize that inadequate optics can produce false negatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testing of alternative hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing rival explanations (e.g., Bastian's pressure hypothesis for preserved tins) by devising direct experiments such as piercing tins under water or applying high pressures to samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept speculative explanations without experimental verification — design targeted experiments to confirm or falsify competing hypotheses (e.g., apply pressure tests, pierce under water to check for inrush/outflow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for sample integrity during handling and transport
rubrics_metrics.description: Observing that flasks cracked or had fragile ends broken during transit and that such breakage admitted air and produced muddiness/contamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor and document physical integrity of samples throughout handling/transport; exclude or treat separately those with mechanical damage as they may be contaminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of substrate-specific exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that some substrates behave differently (e.g., milk putrefied after boiling despite filtered air), so general rules may have exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report and investigate substrate-specific anomalies; do not overgeneralize from a subset of materials — test a range of media and note exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret differences across locations as evidence of external germ sources
rubrics_metrics.description: If identically-prepared infusions behave differently when handled in different localities (one yields life, another remains sterile), infer that some ingredient foreign to the infusion (airborne germs/dust) caused the difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geographical and environmental variation (mountain air vs plain/loft air) as a diagnostic tool to identify airborne particulate sources and to support or refute spontaneous generation claims.
